idiom_name: std::expected decode result + publishing the raw frame to an error exchange via a broker client
implementation_notes: Modern C++ keeps the failure on the normal path: a decoder returns std::expected<Message, DecodeError> (or a std::variant-based Result before C++23), the caller matches on it, and the invalid branch publishes the untouched byte range to the invalid destination - an error exchange binding with rabbitmq-c or AMQP-CPP, or a separate stream. The classic structure survives because the standard library ships no messaging type: the invalid channel is a convention of the client library plus topology, not a language feature. Where a third-party codec throws instead, wrap the decode call in a boundary that converts the exception into the same routing decision so the two paths cannot diverge.
pitfalls: Re-serializing a partially parsed message before routing destroys the evidence; publish the original byte range and keep it alive across the asynchronous publish.
Exceptions from third-party decoders bypass the expected-based path unless the decode boundary catches them - an uncaught one terminates the consumer instead of diverting the message.
A borrowed payload or default-constructed properties in AMQP client libraries may not be copied; the buffer must outlive the publish or the error channel receives garbage.
